text: TLDR: the coached program fails or isn’t coded to notice, or rather, care that its own prescription wasn’t producing the outcome it was designed to produce, with no user facing explanation or attempt to intervene. Your coach is goal- informed, but not nearly as accountable to it and can diverge. While I don’t expect it to override physics, from my perspective, the coach sometimes will outright fail at its job, because the estimation model is intentionally conservative (although there are good reasons why). But the limitation, is that concept takes precedence over anything else. Attempting to fix it takes you through arguably poor UX; resetting separate settings respectively and maybe outside tools/knowledge and foresight to do so. This is added to the fact that the conservative estimates can go for absurd lengths of time, weeks to even months while basically defying the intended goal without intervention, which while easy to fix, is still odd for a premium. $$ This example of the conservatism isn’t an exaggeration: you can practically be in a deficit by a total of a couple pounds over the span of a month, despite your targets intending on a bulk. Comically, the formula will tell you to get back on track on a fresh week, you should eat less than half of a banana on top of the food you already eat. Highly recommend if your fitness status prior to using this app was largely in ignorance to you, you should use your own outside tool to estimate your own initial expenditure while still allowing the app to dynamically adjust. The apps best feature to me is its convenience of logging data; the actual work of applying it, remains on you for a price.

Then compare it to the total number of calories in as defined by MyFitnessPal, and do the math yourself. This is very cumbersome. It also seems to be a very easy fix and would make the app much more effective. The other issue is with entering in food. You cannot select the ounces of food to enter. Instead of changing the units to ounces or grams, and entering in the number of ounces, you need to select 1 oz or grams and then up your servings. So if you’re eating 7 ounces of peaches, you need to 17 servings at 1 ounce each. It’s just silly. Makes the whole process a little confusing and takes extra steps. But unfortunately, after reviewing approximately nine different fitness/tracking apps, this is the closest I’ve come to the original Fitbit app. With so many people upset with what Google Health has done to the Fitbit app, my Fitness pal has a unique opportunity to respond to a market need and create a niche for themselves.

title: Love the idea, but the execution is awful
text: I did a free trial a while ago, but didn’t actually use the app or test any recipes. This week I decided to try using the app again and actually meal plan and prepare the meals, and I noticed several things. 1. I wish the app had an option to continue on a monthly basis instead of choosing 3 months or a year. I unfortunately am cancelling my membership primarily for this reason. 2. The AI doesn’t do a very good job creating lists from the recipes. It was really annoying to have to do the work of ensuring that the grocery items and their respective amounts actually line of with the recipes. From what I understand, that was supposed to be the whole point. But I wound up having to go through the list and manually make several changes. I really feel that I shouldn’t have to edit the grocery list so drastically. Also the fact that it includes recommended wine pairings in the grocery list is an obvious and obnoxious upsell. 3. The recipes don’t offer metric measurements, even though the ingredient list largely goes off of oz. Some of us still prefer to use and kitchen scale in the US, especially when making lists so we know we have the proper ingredient amounts. 4z for some reason when I chose my plan, it charged me twice: once for a yearly plan and once for a 3-month plan. I am still trying to figure out how to get refunded. 5. Some recipes available for 2 people are not available in the family size. It’s fine, but I have to do the math of doubling the recipes myself. Many recipes online allow you to customize based off of how many servings you want. 6. There isn’t a search function on the main page, which makes it hard to look for recipes you haven’t already saved. 7. I did the math on meal just for our lunch and dinner, and if I were to do a full week of recipes it would make our grocery bill astronomical. I ended up doing three recipes each and we’re doubling those in order to not have to buy a gazillion different ingredients each week. This makes it a bit more practical and affordable. I really wish they’d put an approximate cost per meal at the top of each recipe. Overall I loved the idea of this app. It sounded game changing. But it is fundamentally flawed. I’m better off getting a few recipes online and getting my groceries delivered off Walmart. A little extra work, but I’m finding myself working extra with the app regardless.

author: Niknaim is David

title: Great app ruined by ads
text: This app was fantastic before it became Samsung Food. It has been my go-to app for storing recipes and finding new recipes to try for years, and the ease of adding a recipe from an outside source made it that much better. Since it was branded with the Samsung name, the ads have become more and more overbearing. Now I can barely follow any recipe because of the full page ads that take over every 10-15 seconds. At first I thought it was only the recipes that sent you to an external site, but the same format follows no matter where the recipe is found. I’m constantly stopping to close out a full page ad over and over to the point that I have ruined a few recipes because I lose my place and get frustrated with having to close ads to even see the pages. It’s ridiculous. I’m shopping for a new app that I can actually use and will gladly move all my recipes manually and pay for another app if needed to avoid the travesty that has become Samsung Ads…I mean Food.
